title: Baseline Models
learning_outcomes: Explain baseline models and accurately refer to at least two syllabus subtopics.
Apply the main idea of baseline models to a small example, trace, calculation, or scenario.
Identify one important assumption or failure mode and describe how to check it.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study baseline models in the context of machine learning fundamentals. You will connect the PDF subtopics to a small example and practice describing what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Baseline Models matters because it affects how data is collected, represented, analyzed, interpreted, or used in a decision. Check the task and assumptions before choosing a method.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Machine learning estimates patterns from examples. Training is only one step: a robust workflow defines splits, baselines, metrics, assumptions, and monitoring.

items.title: Simple prediction rules
items.text: Define simple prediction rules in relation to baseline models; identify the input, output, assumptions, and who uses the result.

items.title: Majority-class baselines
items.text: Work through majority-class baselines using a small, synthetic example before scaling up. State what the calculation or method returns and why that result is useful.

items.title: Mean and median baselines
items.text: Check the edge cases for mean and median baselines: missing values, unusual ranges, different groups, time boundaries, or a changed input can affect the conclusion.

items.title: Business-rule baselines
items.text: Document the rule or choice for business-rule baselines so another learner can reproduce the analysis and understand its limitations.

items.title: Establishing a meaningful comparison
items.text: Define establishing a meaningful comparison in relation to baseline models; identify the input, output, assumptions, and who uses the result.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Restate the question addressed by baseline models. 2. Identify the input data, intended output, and assumptions. 3. Predict what the small example should show before reading its output. 4. Change one input or assumption, compare the result, and document what remains uncertain.

content_blocks.code:
baseline = [10, 10, 10]
actual = [9, 11, 13]
print("baseline MAE:", round(sum(abs(a-b) for a,b in zip(actual, baseline))/len(actual), 2))

content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the provided synthetic input, rerun or retrace the example, and change one value at a time. Do not use personal records, credentials, or data you are not authorized to access.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Keep the question, data grain, units, and assumptions explicit. If a result differs, inspect the input and steps in order. Avoid turning an observed association into a causal claim, treating a sample as the population, or assuming a small demonstration guarantees production behavior. A complex model is useful only if it improves an appropriate baseline under fair evaluation.

content_blocks.title: Responsible interpretation
content_blocks.text: This example is a teaching aid. It is static in the CodeLeaf lesson and is not executed in the browser. It uses small synthetic values; validate any real workflow in a separate, appropriate local environment and protect sensitive data.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Machine learning estimates patterns from examples. Training is only one step: a robust workflow defines splits, baselines, metrics, assumptions, and monitoring. Record the method, input assumptions, observed result, and one limitation so another person can reproduce and review the work.

task_acceptance_criteria: Refer accurately to the topic and its syllabus subtopics.
Record a reproducible example or a complete manual trace with an expected result.
Document at least one assumption, limitation, data-quality issue, or evaluation check.
hints: Write down the input, expected result, units, and assumptions first.
Change only one condition when testing a revised example.
Ask whether the data and method represent the real decision; do not infer causality or production readiness from a toy example.
troubleshooting: Check input values, path assumptions, package versions, indentation, and units.
For SQL, use a local schema and read-only test data; this page does not provide a live database.
For package-dependent work, create an isolated environment and use the relevant official documentation.
